common_name: Abel Carriere Weigela (Heirloom Rosy-Carmine Weigela with Yellow Throat)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Abel Carriere is a long-cultivated 19th-century French selection grown for its unusually large flowers.

directions: Abel Carriere is one of the oldest named Weigela florida selections still in commerce, prized for flowers noticeably larger than those of most modern cultivars, opening rosy-carmine with a pale yellow-flecked throat in a heavy late-spring flush. The vigorous, arching shrub reaches full size quickly and works well as an informal hedge, screen, or specimen in a mixed border where its old-fashioned, heavy-blooming character stands out against newer compact and reblooming introductions. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest flower display, and prune immediately after flowering since buds form on the current season's new growth. Thin out a few of the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the base of the shrub from becoming congested and woody.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lucifer is a long-established European selection valued for unusually deep, saturated red flower color.

directions: Lucifer forms a dense, rounded shrub covered in late spring and early summer with bell-shaped, deep red flowers that open from pale pink buds, giving a richer, more saturated red than older cultivars like Bristol Ruby. Its compact, well-branched habit suits smaller gardens and mixed borders where a full-sized Weigela florida would be too large, and dark green foliage sets off the red blooms cleanly through the season. Grow in average, well-drained, slightly acid soil in full sun, since flower color and density both improve with more light. Prune hard immediately after the spring bloom flush to maintain a tight shape and encourage strong new growth for the following year's flowers.

common_name: White Knight Weigela (Fragrant Pure White Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; White Knight is grown for pure white, lightly fragrant flowers, a color and trait uncommon among Weigela cultivars.

directions: White Knight produces an unusually heavy covering of pure white, funnel-shaped flowers along the length of its branches in late spring, with the added distinction of a light, pleasant fragrance that most Weigela cultivars lack entirely. A lighter repeat bloom often follows in late summer, extending the display beyond the single spring flush typical of older selections. Its clean green foliage and rounded habit make it a good anchor for a white or pastel-themed border, and the fragrant flowers draw hummingbirds and butterflies as readily as the more common pink and red cultivars. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, and prune right after the main spring flowering since next year's buds form on new growth produced shortly afterward.

common_name: Double Reeves Spirea (Double-Flowered Bridal-Wreath Type Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Double Reeves Spirea is a long-grown double-flowered selection distinct from the Spiraea japonica and S. x vanhouttei bridal-wreath types already common in gardens.

directions: Double Reeves Spirea forms a graceful, fountain-shaped shrub with long, gracefully arching branches that become lined in mid-spring with dense, pompon-like clusters of small, many-petaled double white flowers resembling miniature roses. It blooms earlier in spring and carries noticeably fuller, longer-lasting flower clusters than the related Spiraea x vanhouttei, making it a traditional favorite in Southern and warm-temperate gardens as a specimen, screen, or informal hedge. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, siting it where its wide, weeping spread has room to develop without frequent shearing. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes to the ground right after flowering every few years to keep the arching form youthful and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Garland Spirea is a long-established hybrid of S. thunbergii and S. x multiflora dating to the 1880s, distinct from the S. x vanhouttei and S. nipponica bridal-wreath types already grown widely.

directions: Garland Spirea is one of the earliest spring-blooming spireas, its slender, arching branches smothered from tip to base in clusters of small, pure white flowers that open slightly ahead of the more familiar Vanhoutte spirea and before most of the shrub's narrow, willowy foliage has fully expanded. The dense, fountain-like habit and exceptionally heavy, garland-like bloom make it a classic choice for an informal hedge, foundation planting, or specimen where an unobstructed early-season flower display is wanted. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest flowering; it tolerates a wide range of soils once established. Renewal-prune by removing a portion of the oldest stems at ground level right after bloom, since flowers form on wood from the previous season.

common_name: Dart's Red Spirea (Sterile Deep-Carmine Sport of Anthony Waterer)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dart's Red is a Dutch-raised sport of 'Anthony Waterer' selected for deeper flower color and for not reverting to plain-green shoots.

directions: Dart's Red is a compact, mound-forming sport of the long-popular 'Anthony Waterer', selected in the Netherlands for flat clusters of carmine-red flowers noticeably deeper than its parent's pink-red tone, carried above fine-toothed foliage that emerges red-tinted before settling to blue-green. Unlike some older Spiraea japonica selections, it holds its clean foliage color through the season without throwing the plain-green reverted shoots that can spoil the look of similar cultivars. Its neat, compact habit suits low hedging, mass planting, or the front of a mixed border in a small garden. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest bloom and most compact form, and shear off spent flower clusters to encourage a lighter rebloom later in summer.

common_name: Mt. Fuji Variegated Spirea (Cream-Variegated Thunberg Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Mt. Fuji is a variegated-foliage selection of the early-blooming thunbergii species, distinct from the gold-leaved 'Ogon' already grown widely.

directions: Mt. Fuji carries fine, willow-like leaves irregularly streaked with cream, giving the shrub a soft, variegated texture quite different from the solid gold foliage of 'Ogon' or the plain green of the species, with the variegation holding well through summer before the foliage shifts to yellow and orange tones in fall. Small white flowers open along the slender branches in early spring, typically just ahead of or alongside the unfurling variegated leaves, continuing the thunbergii group's reputation for some of the earliest spirea bloom of the season. Its fine texture and arching form work well as a textural accent or informal low hedge in a mixed border. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since variegation tends to be most pronounced with good light, and renewal-prune older stems after flowering to keep the habit dense.
